Therefore, the total contribution to the response function is given by the anharmonic one-phonon Green function (Figure 2b), the mixed one-two phonon Green function (Figure 2b), and the two-phonon Green function (Figure 2c). Harmonic systems do not have a contribution from mixed Green functions, as phonons cannot decay or scatter during the free propagation.

The expression of the IR (Eq. 102) and Raman (Eq. 107) in the approximation of linear coupling with the probe is equivalent to neglect the diagrams Figure 2(b,c).

Interestingly, the two-phonon propagation gives a non-zero response also in purly harmonic crystals. For example, the harmonic two-phonon IR signal is:

χMα​Mα′(2​p​h)​(ω)=∑a​b​c​d​μ​νeμa​eνb​eμc​eνdma​mb​mc​md​d​𝒵α​ad​Rb​χμ​ν​μ​ν​(ω)​d​𝒵α′​cd​Rd\chi^{(2ph)}_{M_{\alpha}M_{\alpha^{\prime}}}(\omega)=\sum_{abcd\mu\nu}\frac{e_{\mu}^{a}e_{\nu}^{b}e_{\mu}^{c}e_{\nu}^{d}}{\sqrt{m_{a}m_{b}m_{c}m_{d}}}\frac{d\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha a}}{dR_{b}}\chi_{\mu\nu\mu\nu}(\omega)\frac{d\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha^{\prime}c}}{dR_{d}} (108)

where χμ​ν​μ​ν​(ω)\chi_{\mu\nu\mu\nu}(\omega) is the harmonic two-phonon Green function. The interacting two-phonon Green function can be computed within the SSCHA formalism as the response function between quadratic displacements:

𝒜^=ma​mb​(R^a−ℛa)​(R^b−ℛb)\hat{\mathcal{A}}=\sqrt{m_{a}m_{b}}(\hat{R}_{a}-\mathcal{R}_{a})(\hat{R}_{b}-\mathcal{R}_{b}) (109)
ℬ^=ma​mb​(R^c−ℛc)​(R^d−ℛd)\hat{\mathcal{B}}=\sqrt{m_{a}m_{b}}(\hat{R}_{c}-\mathcal{R}_{c})(\hat{R}_{d}-\mathcal{R}_{d}) (110)

Since, in second-quantization formalism, each position operator 𝑹^\hat{\bm{R}} is proportional to the creation-annihilation of one phonon, 𝒜^\hat{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} contain creations and annihilations of two phonons; this is the reason why it is called the two-phonon Green function.

We compute the 𝒑\bm{p} and 𝒒\bm{q} vectors (Eq. 78 and 79) from 𝒜^\hat{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} and insert them into Eq. (83) to get the interacting two-phonon Green functions.

Indeed, if one consider a perfectly harmonic oscillator, we show in Appendix J that the response function coincides with Eq. (96). This is the well-known two-phonon propagator for harmonic systems, and it coincides with the one obtained with the standard many-body approach.

Notably, since usually the non-linear interaction between the probe and the ionic position is small, the diagram Figure 2(b) provides a lower order signal than the two-phonon one (c).

Indeed, all the processes represented in Figure 2 are automatically included in the response function of the TD-SCHA introduced in Sec. IV.1. In principle, also higher-order processes exist, where the probe interacts with more than two phonons. However, the Gaussian constrain on the TD-SCHA density matrix does not allow these excitations; they are accounted within the mean-field approach, affecting the average of the derivatives of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ{\mathcal{B}} observables on the ionic probability distribution, providing a temperature dependency for the vertexes in Figure 2. This is the result of replacing the perturbation V(1)​(𝑹,t)V^{(1)}(\bm{R},t) into Vsc^(1)​(t){\hat{{V_{\text{sc}}}}^{(1)}}(t) in the linear response theory (Eq. 65).

VI Lanczos algorithm to compute the response function

While a numerical implementation to calculate the dynamical one-phonon Green function has been presented[47], its computational cost diverges quickly for systems with more than N=10N=10 atoms, as the self-energy of Eq. (92) requires, for any frequency to probe, the inversion of the matrix

[𝟙−𝑫(4)​(−12​𝝌​(ω))]−1.\left[\mathbbm{1}-\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\bm{\chi}(\omega)\right)\right]^{-1}. (111)

This matrix has a dimension of (3​N)2×(3​N)2(3N)^{2}\times(3N)^{2}; its numerical inversion is a heavy computational task. For example, just to store in memory the matrix of Eq. (111) in a system with 100 atoms with 64-bit floating-point precision, more than 60 Gb are needed. The inversion of Eq. (111) requires a LU decomposition of a matrix of size n=9​N2n=9N^{2}. The LU decomposition scales a n3n^{3}; the overall scaling for computing the inversion is N6N^{6}, which quickly diverges for realistic systems with more than 10 atoms. For this reason, the application of the full dynamical one-phonon Green function has been performed in realistic systems always under the assumption that 𝑫(4)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}=0.

Moreover, as discussed in Sec. V.1, the one-phonon Green function does not provide the most general response to the experimental probe, but it is limited to probes interacting linearly with atomic displacements.

In this section, we derive a very efficient algorithm that allows computing the elements of the response function to any general external perturbation, that is computationally achievable in systems of hundreds of atoms in the full anharmonic regime (even with 𝑫(4)≠0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}\neq 0).

We recall the expression of the response function from Eq. (83):

χ𝒜​ℬ​(ω)=−𝒑​(ℒ+ω2)−1​𝒒\chi_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}(\omega)=-\bm{p}(\mathcal{L}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\bm{q} (112)

where 𝒑\bm{p} and 𝒒\bm{q} are defined in Eq. (78) and Eq. (79) from 𝒜^\hat{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}}.

The algorithm we discuss in this section computes in one shot Eq. (83) for any value of ω\omega. This is an easy task if we use a basis where ℒ\mathcal{L} is tridiagonal (as we show later). Therefore, the purpose of the algorithm is to find the basis on which ℒ\mathcal{L} is tridiagonal.

The bi-conjugate Lanczos algorithm does exactly this job: it builds with an iterative procedure the basis-changing QQ matrix (non-singular) so that:

Q−1​ℒ​Q=𝒯,Q^{-1}\mathcal{L}Q={\mathcal{T}}, (113)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is tridiagonal:

𝒯=(α1γ1⋯0β1α2⋱⋱⋱⋱⋱⋱γn−10⋯βn−1αn){\mathcal{T}}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_{1}&\gamma_{1}&&\cdots&0\\ \beta_{1}&\alpha_{2}&\ddots&&\vdots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\\ \vdots&&\ddots&\ddots&\gamma_{n-1}\\ 0&\cdots&&\beta_{n-1}&\alpha_{n}\end{pmatrix} (114)

The basis (non orthonormal) in which ℒ\mathcal{L} is tridiagonal is represented by the columns of the QQ matrix:

Q=(𝒒1⋯𝒒n)Q=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{q}_{1}}&\cdots&{\bm{q}_{n}}\end{pmatrix} (115)

The rows of the Q−1Q^{-1} matrix define the conjugate vectors:

Q−1=(𝒑1𝒑n).Q^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{p}_{1}}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{p}_{n}}\end{pmatrix}. (116)

The coefficients of the 𝒯\mathcal{T} matrix (the αk\alpha_{k}, βk\beta_{k}, γk\gamma_{k}), the 𝒒k\bm{q}_{k} and 𝒑k\bm{p}_{k} vectors are found with the iterative bi-conjugate Lanczos algorithm[66]:

αk=𝒑𝒌⋅ℒ​𝒒𝒌\alpha_{k}=\bm{p_{k}}\cdot{\mathcal{L}}\bm{q_{k}} (117a)
βk​𝒒𝒌+𝟏=𝒓𝒌=(ℒ−αk)​𝒒𝒌−γk−1​𝒒𝒌−𝟏\beta_{k}\bm{q_{k+1}}=\bm{r_{k}}=(\mathcal{L}-\alpha_{k})\bm{q_{k}}-\gamma_{k-1}\bm{q_{k-1}} (117b)
γk​𝒑𝒌+𝟏=𝒔k=(ℒ†−αk)​𝒑𝒌−βk−1​𝒑𝒌\gamma_{k}\bm{p_{k+1}}=\bm{s}_{k}=({\mathcal{L}}^{\dagger}-\alpha_{k})\bm{p_{k}}-\beta_{k-1}\bm{p_{k}} (117c)
βk=|𝒓𝒌|\beta_{k}=|\bm{r_{k}}| (117d)
γk=𝒔𝒌⋅𝒓𝒌βk\gamma_{k}=\frac{\bm{s_{k}}\cdot\bm{r_{k}}}{\beta_{k}} (117e)

This recursion formally ends either when either 𝒒k\bm{q}_{k} or 𝒑k\bm{p}_{k} are linear combinations of the previous vectors or if 𝒑k⋅𝒒k=0\bm{p}_{k}\cdot\bm{q}_{k}=0. Unless the system is perfectly harmonic, this condition is usually never reached in practical runs, and the algorithm is truncated after a maximum number of steps NmaxN_{\text{max}}.

To facilitate the calculation of the Green function, we initialize the algorithm in the following way:

𝒒𝟏=𝒒|𝒒|\bm{q_{1}}=\frac{\bm{q}}{|\bm{q}|} (118)
𝒑𝟏=𝒑​|𝒒|𝒑⋅𝒒\bm{p_{1}}=\bm{p}\frac{|\bm{q}|}{\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}} (119)

The response function can be rewritten as:

χ𝒜​ℬ(ω)=−(𝒑⋅𝒒)𝒑𝟏⋅(ℒ+ω2)−1𝒒𝟏\chi_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}(\omega)=-({\bm{p}}\cdot{\bm{q}})\;\bm{p_{1}}\cdot(\mathcal{L}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\bm{q_{1}} (120)
χ𝒜​ℬ(ω)=−(𝒑⋅𝒒)𝒑𝟏QQ−1⋅(ℒ+ω2)−1QQ−1𝒒𝟏\chi_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}(\omega)=-({\bm{p}}\cdot{\bm{q}})\;\bm{p_{1}}QQ^{-1}\cdot(\mathcal{L}+\omega^{2})^{-1}QQ^{-1}\bm{q_{1}} (121)

Thanks to the definitions in Eq. (115) and (116) we have

Q−1​𝒒𝟏=(100)Q^{-1}\bm{q_{1}}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ \vdots\\ 0\end{pmatrix} (122)
𝒑𝟏​Q=(10⋯0)\bm{p_{1}}Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&\cdots&0\end{pmatrix} (123)

Thus, the response function is the first element of the inverse matrix in the tridiagonal basis:

χ𝒜​ℬ​(ω)=−(𝒑⋅𝒒)​[(𝒯+ω2)−1]11\chi_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}(\omega)=-({\bm{p}}\cdot{\bm{q}})\left[\left(\mathcal{T}+\omega^{2}\right)^{-1}\right]_{11} (124)

We can compute the first element of the inverse of a tridiagonal matrix as a continued fraction:

χ𝒜​ℬ​(ω)=−(𝒑⋅𝒒)α1+ω2−γ1​β1α2+ω2−γ2​β2⋱\chi_{{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{B}}}(\omega)=\cfrac{-({\bm{p}}\cdot{\bm{q}})}{\alpha_{1}+\omega^{2}-\cfrac{\gamma_{1}\beta_{1}}{\alpha_{2}+\omega^{2}-\cfrac{\gamma_{2}\beta_{2}}{\ddots}}} (125)

Indeed, the application of this method is limited to response functions where the perturbation and the response are not orthogonal, i.e. the product 𝒑⋅𝒒≠0\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}\neq 0. The condition 𝒑⋅𝒒=0\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}=0 is met, for example, by off-diagonal elements of the interacting one-phonon Green function. Luckily, the spectral function depends only on the trace of the interacting one-phonon Green function, so only diagonal elements are required (for which 𝒑⋅𝒒=1\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}=1).

When the recursion is truncated without reaching the stopping condition, we can extend the α\alpha,β\beta and γ\gamma above NstepsN_{\text{steps}} by assuming them as constant:

k≥Nstepsk\geq N_{\text{steps}}
αk=αNmaxβk=βNmaxγk=γNmax.\alpha_{k}=\alpha_{N_{\text{max}}}\qquad\beta_{k}=\beta_{N_{\text{max}}}\qquad\gamma_{k}=\gamma_{N_{\text{max}}}. (126)

Under this hypothesis, the last part of the continued fraction satisfy the self-consistent equation

g⁡(ω)=1αNmax+ω2−γNmax​βNmax​g​(ω),g(\omega)=\frac{1}{\alpha_{N_{\text{max}}}+\omega^{2}-\gamma_{N_{\text{max}}}\beta_{N_{\text{max}}}g(\omega)}, (127)

that is solved:

g⁡(ω)=αNmax+ω22​γNmax​βNmax−(αNmax+ω2)2−4​γNmax​βNmax2​γNmax​βNmax.g(\omega)=\frac{\alpha_{N_{\text{max}}}+\omega^{2}}{2\gamma_{N_{\text{max}}}\beta_{N_{\text{max}}}}-\frac{\sqrt{(\alpha_{N_{\text{max}}}+\omega^{2})^{2}-4\gamma_{N_{\text{max}}}\beta_{N_{\text{max}}}}}{2\gamma_{N_{\text{max}}}\beta_{N_{\text{max}}}}. (128)

This introduces an imaginary term to the Green function when the argument inside the square root becomes negative (branch cut). This termination of the recursion is similar to the proposed one for the turbo Lanczos algorithm in TD-DFT[57]. Additionally, to introduce a finite lifetime, we also add a Lorentzian smearing η\eta by replacing ω→ω+i​η\omega\rightarrow\omega+i\eta; the convergence of the spectrum is achieved as Nsteps→∞N_{\text{steps}}\rightarrow\infty and η→0\eta\rightarrow 0. With this method, we compute the response function at any frequency, with a single tri-diagonalization procedure: the application of ℒ\mathcal{L} to 𝒑i\bm{p}_{i} and 𝒒i\bm{q}_{i} in Eq. (117b) and (117c) is the expensive part of the algorithm. The αi,βi,γi\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},\gamma_{i} coefficients depend on the 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ{\mathcal{B}} observables (on the vectors 𝒑\bm{p} and 𝒒\bm{q} used to start the Lanczos algorithm) but not on the frequency ω\omega. The application of ℒ\mathcal{L} to a vector does not require any matrix inversion; it is efficient and parallelizable. In particular, even if ℒ\mathcal{L} is a dense matrix of [3​N​(1+6​N)]2∼N4[3N(1+6N)]^{2}\sim N^{4} elements (3​N×3​N3N\times 3N the 𝓡\bm{\mathcal{R}} block and 9​N2×9​N29N^{2}\times 9N^{2} both the 𝚼\bm{\Upsilon} and Re​𝑨\mathrm{Re}\bm{A} blocks), the application of ℒ\mathcal{L} to a vector scales as N3N^{3}, much better than the inversion of Eq. (111) (N6N^{6}). In particular, the ℒ\mathcal{L} matrix can be divided into the harmonic and anharmonic contribution:

ℒ=ℒhar+ℒanh,{\mathcal{L}}={\mathcal{L}}^{\text{har}}+{\mathcal{L}}^{\text{anh}}, (129)

where ℒhar{\mathcal{L}}^{\text{har}} is the propagation according to the self-consistent Hamitlonian in equilibrium, while the anharmonic part comes from how the self-consistent Hamiltonian changes under the changes of ρ^(1){{\hat{\rho}}^{(1)}} during the evolution. The harmonic contribution is diagonal in the polarization space (its application to a vector scales as N2N^{2}). In Appendix K, we show that the anharmonic term can be applied to a vector as:

ℒanh​(𝚼~(1)Re~​𝑨(1)𝓡~(1))=(𝚼~​⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)+⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)​𝚼~Re​𝑨~​⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)+⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)​Re​𝑨~−⟨d​𝕍d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)),{\mathcal{L}}^{\text{anh}}\begin{pmatrix}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}\\ {\tilde{\mathrm{Re}}\bm{A}}^{(1)}\\ {\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}+\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}\\ \mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}+\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}\\ -\left\langle\frac{d{\mathbb{V}}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}\end{pmatrix}, (130)

where the average ⟨⋅⟩ρ(1)\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}} is computed on the perturbed ensemble defined by the vector that multiplies ℒanh{\mathcal{L}}^{\text{anh}}, and 𝕍\mathbb{V} is the difference between the BO energy landscape and the potential energy of the equilibrium SSCHA auxiliary Hamiltonian:

𝕍⁡(𝑹)=V⁡(𝑹)−12​∑a​b(Ra−ℛa)​⟨d2​Vd​Ra​d​Rb⟩ρ(0)​(Rb−ℛb).\mathbb{V}(\bm{R})=V(\bm{R})-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ab}(R_{a}-\mathcal{R}_{a})\left\langle\frac{d^{2}V}{dR_{a}dR_{b}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(0)}}(R_{b}-\mathcal{R}_{b}). (131)

Notably, Eq. (130) scales as the matrix product between N×NN\times N matrices, i.e. the overall cost of applying ℒ\mathcal{L} scales with N2N^{2} (in the polarization basis the 𝚼~\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}} and Re​𝑨~\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}} matrices are diagonal). To calculate the full response function, we need to apply the ℒ\mathcal{L} matrix for each iteration. Thus the overall computational cost scales as N2⋅NstepsN^{2}\cdot N_{\text{steps}}, where NstepsN_{\text{steps}} is the number of iterations of the Lanczos algorithm. The computational most expensive part comes from the average

⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1).\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}. (132)

This average is evaluated with a Monte Carlo integration on the stochastic configurations for each element of the matrix. This calculation costs Nconf×N2N_{\text{conf}}\times N^{2} and must be performed at each step. Luckily, this operation runs efficiently in parallel, as the average on the NconfN_{\text{conf}} configurations of the ensemble can be partitioned in separate subsets computed by independent processing units. Notably, within the Lanczos algorithm, there is no difference in the computational cost between computing the bubble only approximation of the self-energy (neglecting 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}} in Eq. 92) or the full expression. We report more details on how Eq. (132) and the transposed of ℒanh{\mathcal{L}}^{\text{anh}} are computed, and how we account for crystal symmetries in Appendix K.

VII Applications

We now illustrate two applications of the TD-SCHA. First, as a simple benchmark, we show how the TD-SCHA performs in a toy model constituted by a single one-dimensional particle in an external anharmonic potential, comparing the results with the exact (numerical) solution of the problem (Sec. VII.1).

Then, we apply the TD-SCHA in linear response regime to a real physical system, the phase III of solid high-pressure hydrogen, and simulate the IR and Raman spectroscopy. This system is challenging for calculating quantum nuclear time-correlation functions ab initio: it is strongly anharmonic, quantum effects are important, and we have many atoms in the simulation cell (N=96N=96).

VII.1 1D particle in an external potential

To benchmark the TD-SCHA, we compare it with the numerical solution of the Schroedinger equation. This is possible only for small systems. In this section, we simulate a one-dimensional particle in a strongly anharmonic external potential. The external potential V⁡(R)V(R) plays the role of Born-Oppenheimer energy landscape, its shape is reported in Figure 3 (a). In Hartree atomic units it is:

V⁡(R)=3​R4+12​R3−3​R2V(R)=3R^{4}+\frac{1}{2}R^{3}-3R^{2} (133)

This example is performed at T=0 KT=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$, where the density matrix is a pure state. Our particle has the mass of an electron. We compare the exact probability distribution of the ground state wave-funciton |ψG​S⟩\ket{\psi_{GS}} (obtained diagonalizing the real Hamiltonian) with the SCHA in Figure 3(a). The SCHA solution is Gaussian, while the exact ground state is a complex function. In Figure 3(b), we present the linear response to a dynamical perturbation. We plot the one-phonon spectral function multiplied by ω\omega, defined as:

𝒮⁡(ω)=−ωπ​Im​𝒢​(ω).{\mathcal{S}}(\omega)=-\frac{\omega}{\pi}\mathrm{Im}\mathcal{G}(\omega). (134)

In this way, 𝒮⁡(ω){\mathcal{S}}(\omega) satisfy the sum rule that its integral is proportional to the number of phonons[31] (the intensity of a peak does not depend on the phonon frequency). We compare the results computed with the harmonic approximation and the TD-SCHA to the exact (numerical) solution.

The exact solution is calculated with the Lehmann representation of the Green function, where we performed the full diagonalization on the Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} to obtain the excited sates |ψi⟩\ket{\psi_{i}}:

𝒢⁡(ω)\displaystyle{\mathcal{G}}(\omega) =∑i=1∞|⟨ψi|m​(R^−ℛ)|ψG​S⟩|2ℏ​ω−Ei+EG​S+i​0++\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\left|\braket{\psi_{i}|\sqrt{m}(\hat{R}-\mathcal{R})|\psi_{GS}}\right|^{2}}{\hbar\omega-E_{i}+E_{GS}+i0^{+}}+
+∑i=1∞|⟨ψi|m​(R^−ℛ)|ψG​S⟩|2ℏ​ω+Ei−EG​S+i​0+\displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\left|\braket{\psi_{i}|\sqrt{m}(\hat{R}-\mathcal{R})|\psi_{GS}}\right|^{2}}{\hbar\omega+E_{i}-E_{GS}+i0^{+}} (135)
ℛ=⟨ψG​S|R^|ψG​S⟩\mathcal{R}=\braket{\psi_{GS}|\hat{R}|\psi_{GS}} (136)

Since we have a 1D system, we can calculate the TD-SCHA response analytically. In particular, we can write the ℒ\mathcal{L} matrix explicitly (Appendix H):

ℒ=(−D(4)2​ωs−2​ωs24​ωs24​ωs​D(3)000D(3)8​ωs20−ωs2)\mathcal{L}=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}}{2\omega_{s}}-2\omega_{s}^{2}&4\omega_{s}^{2}&4\omega_{s}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}\\ 0&0&0\\ \frac{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}}{8\omega_{s}^{2}}&0&-\omega_{s}^{2}\end{pmatrix} (137)

where ωs\omega_{s} is the frequency of the self-consistent harmonic Hamiltonian of the equilibrium SCHA. Since we are at T=0 KT=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ the line of ℒ\mathcal{L} that represent the evolution of Re​A(1)\mathrm{Re}A^{(1)} is zero, as the system is in a pure state. Therefore, Re​A\mathrm{Re}A does not affect the dynamics and we can remove it:

ℒ=(−D(4)2​ωs−2​ωs24​ωs​D(3)D(3)8​ωs2−ωs2)\mathcal{L}=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}}{2\omega_{s}}-2\omega_{s}^{2}&4\omega_{s}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}\\ \frac{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}}{8\omega_{s}^{2}}&-\omega_{s}^{2}\end{pmatrix} (138)

The full anharmonic Green function is:

𝑮⁡(ω)=−(ℒ+ω2)−1\bm{G}(\omega)=-(\mathcal{L}+\omega^{2})^{-1} (139)

The one-phonon Green function 𝒢⁡(ω){\mathcal{G}}(\omega) is the element in the 𝓡\bm{\mathcal{R}} block (the last) of the full Green function 𝑮⁡(ω)\bm{G}(\omega). Performing the inversion analytically we can compute the self-energy:

𝒢​(ω)−1=ω2−ωs2−Π⁡(ω){\mathcal{G}}(\omega)^{-1}=\omega^{2}-\omega_{s}^{2}-\Pi(\omega) (140)
Π⁡(ω)=−D(3)2/(2​ωs)ω2−4​ωs2−D(4)/(2​ωs)\Pi(\omega)=-\frac{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}^{2}/(2\omega_{s})}{\omega^{2}-4\omega_{s}^{2}-\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}/(2\omega_{s})} (141)

As we proved for the general case in Sec. V.1, this self-energy is the same as the one obtained by exploiting the dynamical ansatz formulated in ref.[47]:

Π⁡(ω)=D(3)​(−12​χ​(ω))​[1−D(4)​(−12​χ​(ω))]−1​D(3)\Pi(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\chi(\omega)\right)\left[1-\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\chi(\omega)\right)\right]^{-1}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D} (142)

where in 1D at T=0 KT=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ we have:

χ⁡(ω)=12​ωs2​14​ωs2−ω2\chi(\omega)=\frac{1}{2\omega_{s}^{2}}\frac{1}{4\omega_{s}^{2}-\omega^{2}} (143)

As shown in Figure 3, the strong anharmonicity downshifts the energy of the peak by 50 % of the harmonic result. Here, the TD-SCHA displays a relative error with the exact solution on the phonon energy of 5 %; an important improvement from the 100 % of the harmonic approximation. The TD-SCHA still slightly overestimates the vibrational energy. This is a general feature of the method, as the TD-SCHA wave-function is more rigid than the real one, as we constrained its Gaussian form.

Moreover, the TD-SCHA spectral function displays an overtone, originating from the anharmonic coupling between the oscillations of the average position and the fluctuations. This overtone arises from the pole of the self-energy in Eq. (141). We plot, in Figure 4, the spectral function zoomed in the energy region where the overtone appears. In this example, it is 100 times smaller than the principal peak. This is a consequence that the overtone is off-resonant: there are not one-phonon excitations in resonance. The TD-SCHA correctly reproduces the overtone intensity but with a relative error on its energy of 60%.

Interestingly, the energy of the overtone is not twice the energy of the fundamental phonon mode, as there is a very strong anharmonicity. The TD-SCHA is unable to simulate third or higher overtones, as we have only two poles from the Green function that are the zeros of the determinant of the inverse of 𝑮⁡(ω)\bm{G}(\omega).

Finally, we can simulate the wave-function dynamics adding a time-dependent external potential in a nonlinear regime. For this purpose, we integrate the TD-SCHA equation of motion and compare the result with the exact evolution. We introduce, at t0=0t_{0}=0, a perturbation of the form:

V(1)​(R,t)=E0​R​sin⁡(ω0​t)V^{(1)}(R,t)=E_{0}R\sin(\omega_{0}t) (144)

where E0=1​Ha/BohrE_{0}=1\,\text{Ha/Bohr}, and ω0=1\omega_{0}=1 Ha. The results are shown in Figure 5.

The TD-SCHA time evolution is very close to the exact dynamics in the first oscillations, where the wave-function is well localized. The two solutions deviate when the exact wave-function becomes delocalized at around 7 atomic units: The TD-SCHA probability distribution is more localized during the whole dynamics, as shown by the mean square displacement reported in Figure 5(d). However, even after that time, the accuracy of the TD-SCHA evolution is good. This shows how the TD-SCHA can reproduce well the nuclear dynamics even in the nonlinear regime.

VII.2 High-pressure hydrogen

In this section, we employ the linear response theory of the TD-SCHA to calculate the Raman and spectra of high-pressure hydrogen phase III. The simulation of vibrational spectra in high-pressure phases of molecular hydrogen is very important to dissect the crystal geometry, as it is the only experimental signature directly related to the lattice. Both X-ray spectroscopy and neutron scattering are extremely challenging for the small samples of hydrogen available. Thus, the structure identification is possible only by comparing results from ab initio simulations with experimental data. We already presented these results and deeply discussed their relevance and implications in ref.[35]. Here, instead, we focus on the details of the calculation of the Raman and IR response at 260 GPa260\text{\,}\mathrm{GPa} (T=0 KT=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$). Hydrogen phase III is a monoclinic crystal of symmetry group C2/c, with 24 atoms in the primitive cell.

We computed only the one-phonon contribution to the full response function: we approximate the Raman tensor as independent from the ionic displacement equal to the value on the SCHA equilibrium positions, as described in Sec. V.2 and V.3. The simulations are performed on a 2x2x1 supercell to sample the Brillouin zone for phonons (96 atoms). The ab initio energy landscape is simulated through DFT, with the BLYP[67] functional. For all the DFT calculations, we employed the Quantum ESPRESSO[68, 69] package, with a plane wave basis set and a norm-conserving pseudo-potential from the Pseudo Dojo library[70]. The energy cutoff for the basis of the wave-functions was 60 Ry (240 Ry for the electronic density). The Brillouin zone for electrons is sampled on a 4x4x4 mesh in the phonon displaced supercell (2x2x1). The Raman tensor is obtained with linear response DFT as implemented in the PHonon package of quantum ESPRESSO within LDA[43].

In Figure 6 we compute the Raman spectra progressively switching on anharmonicity. In Figure 6(a), we show the harmonic Raman spectra, computed within perturbation theory. We present in Figure 6(b) the Raman spectra of the SCHA equilibrium self-consistent harmonic Hamiltonian (Eq. 26). Here, phonons have an infinite lifetime, as in the harmonic case. However, the peak positions and intensities are already strongly affected by anharmonicity through the equilibrium SCHA self-consistency. This response is the phonon spectra presented in the original derivation of the static SCHA[29, 71, 72]. Indeed, phonons defined from the self-consistent harmonic Hamiltonian of the equilibrium density (the SSCHA auxiliary phonons) are not the correct dynamical response. To get the Raman spectrum, one has to calculate the dynamical response function, as introduced in Sec. IV.1. In Figure 6(c,d), we report the anharmonic Raman spectrum calculated within TD-SCHA and the Lanczos algorithm introduced in Sec. VI. We compute the Raman signal within the bubble approximation in Figure 6(c), where we neglect four-phonon scattering processes in the expression of the self-energy (Eq. 92). This is equivalent to account only for the bubble dyagram of Figure 1(a) replacing the interacting two-phonon propagator with the non interacting one. This is the standard way of computing dynamical properties starting from the SCHA and similar methods, as commonly done in TDEP[58], and ALAMODE[59]. In Figure 6(d) we report the full dynamical response within TD-SCHA beyond the bubble approximation. Notably, the Raman signal strongly changes when we account for the full anharmonicity, both in the vibron (that acquires a higher line-width and non-Lorentzian shape) and low-energy phonons. Our Lanczos algorithm enables for the first time to systematically overcome the “bubble” approximation.

The downshift of the vibron peak (the strongest peak in the spectrum at high frequencies) from the Harmonic (Figure 6a) to the full anharmonic spectrum (Figure 6d) occurs already when considering equilibrium self-consistent harmonic phonons. The vibron acquires a finite lifetime when we calculate the response function with the Lanczos, deviating from the Lorentzian shape. We report the comparison with experimental data, obtained under similar conditions[73]. More details on the comparison with experiments have been extensively discussed elsewhere[35]. In particular, the bubble only approximation matches better the experimental data than the full TD-SCHA expression. However, this is an artifact of the DFT functional (BLYP) used to represent the nuclear energy landscape, which exasperates the quantum melting and dissociation of the H2\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} molecules under pressure[35, 74]. Thus the apparent good agreement of Bubble only is due to an error cancellation between higher order anharmonicity and the exchange correlation error in the DFT simulation. We report also the simulation of the IR and the comparison with experiments[73] in Figure 7.

In Figure 8 we report how the Raman spectrum depends on the number of iterations in the Lanczos algorithm. As we increase the number of Lanczos iterations the spectrum gets refined. To converge, we must do the limit η→0\eta\rightarrow 0 and Nsteps→∞N_{\text{steps}}\rightarrow\infty; each step introduces a new pole in the Green function and a peak in the spectrum. When the distance between peaks is smaller than the smearing, the spectrum becomes smooth and does not change if we add more iterations.

When the number of iterations is small, the use of a terminator (introduced in Sec. VI) strongly improves the convergence with lower values of η\eta. However, when the number of iterations is several hundred, it does not affect the spectral function.

Since the energy of the vibron is more than 3000 cm−13000\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-1}, the temperature needed to populate excited states is above 4000 K4000\text{\,}\mathrm{K}. There is no hope to simulate this lattice vibration with standard AIMD, that neglects quantum fluctuations. For this reason, previous studies on high-pressure hydrogen that neglected quantum effects reported a much more modest anharmonicity in the Raman signal[75, 76].

These results indicate that the linear response of TD-SCHA can tackle complex open physical problems from first principles, providing an unprecedented precision on the evaluation of dynamical correlation functions that is sufficient to compare with experimental results[35].

VIII Conclusions

In this work, we introduced a new time-dependent theory for lattice dynamics based on the self-consistent harmonic approximation that can be applied to real systems with a first-principle treatment of the electrons. We discussed the linear response on the static SCHA equilibrium solution of the new equations and derived an efficient algorithm that computes the response function at any frequency with a single calculation. This algorithm, with the simple knowledge of two observables of ionic positions, can compute efficiently time-correlation function, with the inclusion of thermal and quantum effects. Notably, this result is not empirical but derived from a grounded basis: the least action principle. We benchmark the theory both in a simple strongly anharmonic one-dimensional case and on phase III of solid hydrogen, a real complex molecular crystal, with ab initio treatment of electrons.

The theory proved able to accurately reproduce complex phonon line-widths that arise from strong anharmonic coupling. The TD-SCHA paves the way to predict from first-principles the outcome of most experiments that probe the lattice dynamics, like IR and Raman spectroscopy, Neutron, and X-Ray scattering. The theory can be employed in strongly anharmonic regimes, even when quantum fluctuations are dominant and where perturbative approach fails, as in cryogenic conditions, when light ions are present, or in systems close to a second order structural phase transition, as multiferroics, charge density waves, ferroelectrics and thermoelectric materials. Moreover, TD-SCHA describes also out-of-equilibrium dynamics, enabling the study of chemical reactions with light atoms, as the proton transfer in biomolecules, and the simulation of pump-probe spectroscopies.

Appendix A Equilibrium

In this appendix we show that, among all possible stationary density matrices in Eq. (22), the one that minimizes the functional:

F=E−T​SF=E-TS

is the SCHA solution, i.e. the one where temperature is uniform on all the degrees of freedom.

Since we are in a stationary solution, we can write everything in the basis of 𝒆𝝁\bm{e_{\mu}} vectors that diagonalizes the 𝚼\bm{\Upsilon}, 𝑨\bm{A} and ⟨∂2V/∂𝑹~2⟩ρ\left\langle\partial^{2}V/\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}^{2}\right\rangle_{\rho}.

The FF functional is:

F⁡[ρ^]=⟨K^+V^⟩ρ^−T​S​[ρ^]F[\hat{\rho}]=\left\langle\hat{K}+\hat{V}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}}-TS[\hat{\rho}] (145)

The average of the kinetic energy (Eq. 195) is:

⟨K^⟩ρ^=ℏ22​∑μ(Υ~μ4+A~μ)\left\langle\hat{K}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}\sum_{\mu}\left(\frac{\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\mu}}{4}+\tilde{A}_{\mu}\right) (146)

Substituting Eq. (217b), we get:

⟨K^⟩ρ^=∑μℏ​ωμ​(2​nμ+1)4\left\langle\hat{K}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}}=\sum_{\mu}\frac{\hbar\omega_{\mu}(2n_{\mu}+1)}{4} (147)

The entropy S⁡[ρ^]S[\hat{\rho}] can be obtained as the sum of the entropies of the Harmonic oscillators on the μ\mu modes:

S=kb2​∑μ[βμ​ℏ​ωμtanh⁡βμ​ℏ​ω2−2​log⁡(sinh⁡βμ​ℏ​ωμ2)]S=\frac{k_{b}}{2}\sum_{\mu}\left[\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega_{\mu}}{\tanh\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega}{2}}-2\log\left(\sinh\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega_{\mu}}{2}\right)\right] (148)

We must impose that

∂F∂βμ=0\frac{\partial F}{\partial\beta_{\mu}}=0 (149)
∂⟨K^⟩∂βμ+∂⟨V^⟩∂βμ−T​∂S∂βμ=0\frac{\partial\braket{\hat{K}}}{\partial\beta_{\mu}}+\frac{\partial\braket{\hat{V}}}{\partial\beta_{\mu}}-T\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_{\mu}}=0 (150)
∂⟨K^⟩∂βμ=−ℏ2​ωμ28​sinh2⁡(βμ​ℏ​ωμ2)\frac{\partial\braket{\hat{K}}}{\partial\beta_{\mu}}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}\omega_{\mu}^{2}}{8\sinh^{2}\left(\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega_{\mu}}{2}\right)} (151)

The derivative of the average of the potential can be computed exploiting the formalism introduced by Bianco et al.[47]. In particular, they showed that the derivative of any observable with respect to a the quantum fluctuations is:

∂⟨V⁡(𝑹)⟩ρ∂Υμ=12​∑a​b∂Υ~−1a​b∂Υμ​⟨∂2V∂R~a​∂R~b⟩ρ\frac{\partial\left\langle V(\bm{R})\right\rangle_{\rho}}{\partial\Upsilon_{\mu}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ab}\frac{\partial{{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{-1}}_{ab}}{\partial\Upsilon_{\mu}}\left\langle\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{R}_{a}\partial\tilde{R}_{b}}\right\rangle_{\rho} (152)

We can write it in the polarization basis (exploiting Eq. (217b):

∂⟨V⁡(𝑹)⟩ρ∂Υμ=−12​Υ~μ−2​ωμ2\frac{\partial\left\langle V(\bm{R})\right\rangle_{\rho}}{\partial\Upsilon_{\mu}}=-\frac{1}{2}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\mu}^{-2}\omega_{\mu}^{2} (153)

From which we get the average of the potential:

∂⟨V⁡(𝑹)⟩ρ∂βμ=−ℏ2​ωμ28​sinh2⁡(βμ​ℏ​ωμ2)\frac{\partial\left\langle V(\bm{R})\right\rangle_{\rho}}{\partial\beta_{\mu}}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}\omega_{\mu}^{2}}{8\sinh^{2}\left(\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega_{\mu}}{2}\right)} (154)

While the derivative of the entropy is:

∂S∂βμ=−βμ​ℏ2​ωμ2​kb4​sinh2⁡(βμ​ℏ​ωμ2)\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_{\mu}}=-\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar^{2}\omega_{\mu}^{2}k_{b}}{4\sinh^{2}\left(\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega_{\mu}}{2}\right)} (155)

Putting all together we get:

2​ℏ2​ωμ2−kb​T​2​βμ​ℏ2​ωμ28​sinh2⁡(βμ​ℏ​ωμ2)=0\frac{2\hbar^{2}\omega_{\mu}^{2}-k_{b}T2\beta_{\mu}\hbar^{2}\omega_{\mu}^{2}}{8\sinh^{2}\left(\frac{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega_{\mu}}{2}\right)}=0 (156)

And we get the condition that βμ\beta_{\mu} must satisfy to minimize the free energy:

βμ=1kb​T\beta_{\mu}=\frac{1}{k_{b}T} (157)

Appendix D Energy conservation

Here we show that the TD-SCHA equation of motion (Eq. 41) satisfies energy conservation when we switch off the time-dependent perturbation, as we expect from a closed system. This is not trivial: it does not happen in other methods for finite temperature dynamics of ions, as the finite temperature multi-configurational time-dependent Hartree method[77].

The total energy is computed as the average of the BO Hamiltonian on the time-dependent density matrix:

E⁡(t)=⟨H^⟩ρ^​(t)=Tr⁡[ρ^​(t)​H^].E(t)=\left\langle\hat{H}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)}=\tr\left[\hat{\rho}(t)\hat{H}\right]. (193)

By dividing into kinetic and potential contribution, the total energy is:

E⁡(t)=⟨K^⟩ρ^​(t)+⟨V^⟩ρ^​(t)E(t)=\left\langle\hat{K}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)}+\left\langle\hat{V}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)} (194)

The kinetic energy can be evaluated analytically directly from the density matrix of Eq. (43):

⟨K^⟩ρ^​(t)=ℏ22[\displaystyle\left\langle\hat{K}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}\bigg[ Tr⁡(4​𝑪~​(𝚼~)−1​𝑪~−Im​𝑨~​(𝚼~)−1​Im​𝑨~)+\displaystyle\tr\bigg(4\tilde{\bm{C}}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\tilde{\bm{C}}-\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}\bigg)+
−2​Tr⁡(𝑪~​(𝚼~)−1​Im​𝑨~)+\displaystyle-2\tr\bigg(\tilde{\bm{C}}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}\bigg)+
+14Tr𝚼~+Tr𝑨~]+∑i=1nℏ2​Qi22​mi\displaystyle+\frac{1}{4}\tr\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}+\tr\tilde{\bm{A}}\bigg]+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\hbar^{2}Q_{i}^{2}}{2m_{i}} (195)

Also here, we dropped the explicit time dependency of the parameters that represent ρ^​(t)\hat{\rho}(t).

The last term is the kinetic energy of classical particles, the rest is the contribution of the quantum and thermal fluctuations to the kinetic energy.

To prove that dd​t​E​(t)=0\frac{d}{dt}E(t)=0, we compute the derivative of the average kinetic energy:

d​⟨K^⟩ρ^​(t)d​t\displaystyle\frac{d\left\langle\hat{K}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)}}{dt} =ℏ22[14Trd​𝚼~d​t+∑i=13​nQimid​Qid​t+\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}\bigg[\frac{1}{4}\tr\frac{d\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}{dt}+\sum_{i=1}^{3n}\frac{Q_{i}}{m_{i}}\frac{dQ_{i}}{dt}+
+2​Tr⁡(4​𝑪~​(𝚼~)−1​d​𝑪~d​t−𝑪~​(Υ~)−1​d​Im​𝑨~d​t)+\displaystyle+2\tr\left(4\tilde{\bm{C}}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\frac{d{\tilde{\bm{C}}}}{dt}-\tilde{\bm{C}}(\tilde{\Upsilon})^{-1}\frac{d\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}}{dt}\right)+
+Tr⁡d​Re​𝑨~d​t−2​Tr⁡(d​𝑪~d​t​(𝚼~)−1​Im​𝑨~)+\displaystyle+\tr\frac{d\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}}{dt}-2\tr\left(\frac{d\tilde{\bm{C}}}{dt}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}\right)+
−2​Tr⁡(Im​𝑨~​(𝚼~)−1​Im​𝑨~˙+𝑪~​d​(𝚼~)−1d​t​Im​𝑨~)+\displaystyle-2\tr\left(\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\dot{\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}}+\tilde{\bm{C}}\frac{d(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}}{dt}\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}\right)+
+Tr(4𝑪~d​(𝚼~)−1d​t𝑪~−Im𝑨~d​(𝚼~)−1d​tIm𝑨~)].\displaystyle+\tr\left(4\tilde{\bm{C}}\frac{d(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}}{dt}\tilde{\bm{C}}-\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}\frac{d(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}}{dt}\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}\right)\bigg]. (196)

By substituting the equation of motion (Eq. 49e) we get the final derivative of the kinetic energy:

d​⟨K^⟩ρ^​(t)d​t\displaystyle\frac{d\left\langle\hat{K}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)}}{dt} =∑iℏ​Qi​⟨fi⟩ρmi+\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{\hbar Q_{i}\left\langle f_{i}\right\rangle_{\rho}}{m_{i}}+
+2​ℏ​Tr⁡[⟨∂2V∂𝑹~​∂𝑹~⟩ρ⁡(t)​(𝚼~)−1​𝑪~]+\displaystyle+2\hbar\tr\left[\left\langle\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho(t)}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\tilde{\bm{C}}\right]+
−ℏ​Tr⁡[⟨∂2V∂𝑹~​∂𝑹~⟩ρ⁡(t)​(𝚼~)−1​Im​𝑨~]\displaystyle-\hbar\tr\left[\left\langle\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho(t)}(\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}})^{-1}\mathrm{Im}\tilde{\bm{A}}\right] (197)

In the same way, we can compute the derivative of the average potential:

d​⟨V^⟩ρ^​(t)d​t=−∑a​b⟨(Ra−ℛa)(Rb−ℛb)V⟩ρ⁡(t)12d​Υa​bd​t+\displaystyle\frac{d\left\langle\hat{V}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)}}{dt}=-\sum_{ab}\left\langle(R_{a}-\mathcal{R}_{a})(R_{b}-\mathcal{R}_{b})V\right\rangle_{\rho(t)}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt}+
+∑a​b⟨(Ra−ℛa)V⟩ρ⁡(t)Υa​bd​ℛbd​t+⟨V⟩ρ⁡(t)1𝒩d​𝒩d​t\displaystyle+\sum_{ab}\left\langle(R_{a}-\mathcal{R}_{a})V\right\rangle_{\rho(t)}\Upsilon_{ab}\frac{d\mathcal{R}_{b}}{dt}+\left\langle V\right\rangle_{\rho(t)}\frac{1}{{\mathcal{N}}}\frac{d{\mathcal{N}}}{dt} (198)

By substituting the equation of motion and integrating by parts the averages, it is possible to show that:

dd​t​⟨V⟩ρ^​(t)=−dd​t​⟨K⟩ρ^​(t)\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle V\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)}=-\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle K\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}(t)} (199)

To finally prove this equation, we calculate the time derivative of the average potential (Eq. 198), showing that it balances the time derivative of the average kinetic energy, proving that the total energy is conserved by the equation of motions.

For this purpose, we use formalism introduced by Bianco et al[47] (appendix C, Eq. C1): given an observable O⁡(𝑹)O(\bm{R}), the average of its derivative can be written as:

⟨d​Od​Ra⟩ρ=∑bΥa​b​⟨(Rb−ℛb)​O⟩ρ\left\langle\frac{dO}{dR_{a}}\right\rangle_{\rho}=\sum_{b}\Upsilon_{ab}\left\langle(R_{b}-\mathcal{R}_{b})O\right\rangle_{\rho} (200)

For this reason, we can write:

∑a​bd​ℛbd​tΥa​b⟨(Ra−ℛa)V⟩ρ=−∑bd​ℛbd​t⟨fa(𝑹)⟩ρ\sum_{ab}\frac{d\mathcal{R}_{b}}{dt}\Upsilon_{ab}\left\langle(R_{a}-\mathcal{R}_{a})V\right\rangle_{\rho}=-\sum_{b}\frac{d\mathcal{R}_{b}}{dt}\left\langle f_{a}(\bm{R})\right\rangle_{\rho} (201)

For simplicity, we define 𝒖=(𝑹−𝓡)\bm{u}=(\bm{R}-\bm{\mathcal{R}}). The other term of Eq. (198) is

∑a​b⟨ua​ub​V⟩ρ​12​d​Υa​bd​t\displaystyle\sum_{ab}\left\langle u_{a}u_{b}V\right\rangle_{\rho}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt} =∑a​b​c​d⟨uc​ub​V⟩ρ​Υc​d​Υd​a−1​12​d​Υa​bd​t\displaystyle=\sum_{abcd}\left\langle u_{c}u_{b}V\right\rangle_{\rho}\Upsilon_{cd}\Upsilon^{-1}_{da}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt}
=∑a​b​d⟨d⁡(ub​V)d​Rd⟩ρ​Υd​a−1​12​d​Υa​bd​t\displaystyle=\sum_{abd}\left\langle\frac{d(u_{b}V)}{dR_{d}}\right\rangle_{\rho}\Upsilon^{-1}_{da}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt} (202)

The derivative gives:

∑a​b⟨ua​ub​V⟩ρ​12​d​Υa​bd​t\displaystyle\sum_{ab}\left\langle u_{a}u_{b}V\right\rangle_{\rho}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt} =∑a​b⟨V⟩ρ​Υb​a−1​12​d​Υa​bd​t+\displaystyle=\sum_{ab}\left\langle V\right\rangle_{\rho}\Upsilon^{-1}_{ba}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt}+
+∑a​b​d⟨ubd​Vd​Rd⟩ρΥd​a−112d​Υa​bd​t\displaystyle+\sum_{abd}\left\langle u_{b}\frac{dV}{dR_{d}}\right\rangle_{\rho}\Upsilon^{-1}_{da}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt} (203)

The first term is zero, because:

∑a​bΥb​a−1​d​Υa​bd​t=12​dd​t​Tr​[𝚼−1​𝚼]=0\sum_{ab}\Upsilon^{-1}_{ba}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\textup{Tr}\left[\bm{\Upsilon}^{-1}\bm{\Upsilon}\right]=0 (204)

While for the second term we can proceed again:

∑a​b⟨ua​ub​V⟩ρ​12​d​Υa​bd​t=∑a​b​c​d​e⟨ue​d​Vd​Rd⟩ρ​Υe​c​Υc​b−1​Υd​a−1​12​d​Υa​bd​t\sum_{ab}\left\langle u_{a}u_{b}V\right\rangle_{\rho}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt}=\sum_{abcde}\left\langle u_{e}\frac{dV}{dR_{d}}\right\rangle_{\rho}\Upsilon_{ec}\Upsilon^{-1}_{cb}\Upsilon^{-1}_{da}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt} (205)
∑a​b⟨ua​ub​V⟩ρ​12​d​Υa​bd​t=∑a​b​c​d⟨d2​Vd​Rc​d​Rd⟩ρ​Υc​b−1​Υd​a−1​12​d​Υa​bd​t\sum_{ab}\left\langle u_{a}u_{b}V\right\rangle_{\rho}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt}=\sum_{abcd}\left\langle\frac{d^{2}V}{dR_{c}dR_{d}}\right\rangle_{\rho}\Upsilon^{-1}_{cb}\Upsilon^{-1}_{da}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\Upsilon_{ab}}{dt} (206)

Introducing the mass re-scaled for 𝚼−1\bm{\Upsilon}^{-1}:

Υ~a​b−1=ma​mb​Υa​b−1,{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{-1}_{ab}=\sqrt{m_{a}m_{b}}\Upsilon^{-1}_{ab}, (207)

we get the final equivalence:

12​Tr​[⟨𝒖⊗𝒖​V⟩ρ​d​𝚼d​t]=12​Tr​[⟨d2​Vd​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ​𝚼~−1​𝚼~−1​d​𝚼~d​t].\frac{1}{2}\textup{Tr}\left[\left\langle\bm{u}\otimes\bm{u}V\right\rangle_{\rho}\frac{d\bm{\Upsilon}}{dt}\right]=\frac{1}{2}\textup{Tr}\left[\left\langle\frac{d^{2}V}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{-1}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}^{-1}}\frac{d\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}{dt}\right]. (208)

Substituting Eq. (201) and (208) into Eq. (198), and substituting the equation of motion, it is easy to show that

dd​t​⟨K^⟩ρ⁡(t)=−dd​t​⟨V^⟩ρ⁡(t)\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle\hat{K}\right\rangle_{\rho(t)}=-\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle\hat{V}\right\rangle_{\rho(t)}

Appendix E Entropy conservation

The entropy defined on the many-body density matrix is:

S⁡[ρ^​(t)]=−kb​Tr⁡[ρ^​(t)​log⁡ρ^​(t)]S[\hat{\rho}(t)]=-k_{b}\tr\left[\hat{\rho}(t)\log\hat{\rho}(t)\right] (209)

for simplicity, we drop the explicit tt dependence of ρ^​(t)\hat{\rho}(t).

B⁡(ρ^)=ρ^​log⁡ρ^B(\hat{\rho})=\hat{\rho}\log\hat{\rho} (210)
d​Sd​t=−kb​Tr⁡[d​ρ^d​t​d​B​(ρ^)d​ρ^]\frac{dS}{dt}=-k_{b}\tr\left[\frac{d\hat{\rho}}{dt}\frac{dB(\hat{\rho})}{d\hat{\rho}}\right] (211)
d​Sd​t=i​kbℏ​[Tr⁡(ℋ^​[ρ]​ρ^​d​B​(ρ^)d​ρ^)−Tr⁡(ρ^​ℋ^​[ρ]​d​B​(ρ^)d​ρ^)]\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{ik_{b}}{\hbar}\left[\tr\left({\hat{\mathcal{H}}}[\rho]\hat{\rho}\frac{dB(\hat{\rho})}{d\hat{\rho}}\right)-\tr\left(\hat{\rho}{\hat{\mathcal{H}}}[\rho]\frac{dB(\hat{\rho})}{d\hat{\rho}}\right)\right] (212)

By exploiting the cyclic permutation of the trace and the commutation between d​B​(ρ^)/d​ρ^dB(\hat{\rho})/d\hat{\rho} and ρ^\hat{\rho}, Eq. (212) is zero.

Appendix F Steady state solutions

Substituting Eq. (60) inside Eq. (49e) we get the following conditions:

⟨fa⟩ρ=0\left\langle f_{a}\right\rangle_{\rho}=0 (213a)
12​ℏ​⟨∂2V∂R~a​∂R~b⟩ρ=ℏ2​(14​Θ~a​b2−Re​A~a​b2)\frac{1}{2\hbar}\left\langle\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{R}_{a}\partial\tilde{R}_{b}}\right\rangle_{\rho}=\frac{\hbar}{2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\tilde{\Theta}_{ab}^{2}-\mathrm{Re}{\tilde{A}}^{2}_{ab}\right) (213b)

Eq. (213a) is a necessary condition for the equilibrium SCHA: the average of the BO forces is the gradient of the SCHA free energy versus the centroids positions 𝓡\bm{\mathcal{R}}[29]. Moreover, from Eq. (49d) we have that 𝚯~\tilde{\bm{\Theta}} and Re​𝑨~\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}} commute in the static solution, from which also 𝚼~\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}} and Re​𝑨~\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}} commute (that is a direct consequence of the commutation between ρ^\hat{\rho} and ℋ^​[ρ]{\hat{\mathcal{H}}}[\rho]). Since it is better to express our quantity as a function of the total dispersion 𝚼~\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}} (Eq. 45) we have:

𝚼~24+𝚼~​Re​𝑨~=1ℏ2​⟨∂2V∂𝑹~​∂𝑹~⟩ρ.\frac{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}^{2}}{4}+\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}=\frac{1}{\hbar^{2}}\left\langle\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho}. (214)

If we express Eq. (214) in the basis that diagonalizes both 𝚼~\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}} and Re​𝑨~\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}, the same basis must diagonalize also ⟨∂2V∂𝑹~​∂𝑹~⟩\braket{\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}}}. Let us define 𝒆𝝁\bm{e_{\mu}} the eigenvector of ⟨∂2V∂𝑹~​∂𝑹~⟩\braket{\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}\partial\tilde{\bm{R}}}}, 𝚼~\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}} and Re​𝑨~\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}} and ωμ2\omega_{\mu}^{2}, Υ~μ\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\mu} and Re​A~μ\mathrm{Re}\tilde{A}_{\mu} the corresponding eigenvalues:

∑b⟨∂2V∂R~a​∂R~b⟩ρ​eμb=ωμ2​eμa,\sum_{b}\left\langle\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\tilde{R}_{a}\partial\tilde{R}_{b}}\right\rangle_{\rho}e_{\mu}^{b}=\omega_{\mu}^{2}e_{\mu}^{a}, (215)

Eq. (214) becomes:

Υ~μ24+Υ~μ​Re​A~μ=ωμ2ℏ2.\frac{\tilde{\Upsilon}^{2}_{\mu}}{4}+\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\mu}\mathrm{Re}\tilde{A}_{\mu}=\frac{\omega_{\mu}^{2}}{\hbar^{2}}. (216)

Without loss of generality, if we change variable introducing a new parameter nμn_{\mu} and define:

Υ~μ=2​ωμℏ​(2​nμ+1),\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\mu}=\frac{2\omega_{\mu}}{\hbar(2n_{\mu}+1)}, (217a)
from Eq. (216), we get:
Re​A~μ=2​ωμ​nμ​(nμ+1)ℏ​(2​nμ+1).\mathrm{Re}\tilde{A}_{\mu}=\frac{2\omega_{\mu}n_{\mu}(n_{\mu}+1)}{\hbar(2n_{\mu}+1)}. (217b)

In these equations, nμn_{\mu} is a free parameter for each frequency: the TD-SCHA equations are stationary for any choice of nμn_{\mu}. In particular, we can write nμn_{\mu} as the Bose-Einstein occupation number with a temperature that depends on μ\mu:

nμ=1eβμ​ℏ​ωμ−1n_{\mu}=\frac{1}{e^{\beta_{\mu}\hbar\omega_{\mu}}-1} (218)

The stationary density matrix identified by Eq. (217b) and (60) is the product of equilibrium densities matrices of harmonic oscillators of frequencies ωμ\omega_{\mu} and temperatures βμ\beta_{\mu}.

Here, we apply perturbation theory on the TD-SCHA equations for small perturbations. Starting from this paragraph through the rest of the paper, we drop the (0) index and all the quantities without (1) or the explicit time dependency refer to equilibrium quantities. Since we are expanding around equilibrium solutions, we have:

𝑪=0𝑸=0Im​𝑨=0\bm{C}=0\qquad\bm{Q}=0\qquad\mathrm{Im}\bm{A}=0 (219)

When t≥t0t\geq t_{0}, we add an external time dependent perturbation to the non interacting potential:

Even if Re​𝑨~​(t)\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}(t) does not affect the average of the observable directly, we need to keep it, as 𝚼⁡(t)\bm{\Upsilon}(t) depends explicitly on its dynamics. In Eq. (241c), the bar ⋅¯\bar{\cdot} over a symbol indicates a tensor. 𝑿¯\bar{\bm{X}}, 𝒀¯\bar{\bm{Y}}, 𝑿′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}, and 𝒀′¯\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}} are 4-rank tensors, 𝒁¯\bar{\bm{Z}}, 𝒁′¯\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}}, and 𝑿′′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}} are 3-rank tensors, while 𝒁′′¯\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime\prime}} is a 2-rank tensor. We recall that 𝚼~(1)\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}^{(1)} and Re​𝑨~(1)\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}^{(1)} are 2-rank tensor, as well as 𝒇Υ(1)\bm{f}_{\Upsilon}^{(1)} and 𝒇Re​A(1)\bm{f}_{\mathrm{Re}A}^{(1)}, while 𝓡(1)\bm{\mathcal{R}}^{(1)} and 𝒇ℛ(1)\bm{f}_{\mathcal{R}}^{(1)} are vectors (1-rank).

The product between tensors is the defined by the operator on the left. 4-rank tensors 𝑿¯\bar{\bm{X}}, 𝒀¯\bar{\bm{Y}}, 𝑿′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}, and 𝒀′¯\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}} are contracted on the last two indices:

(𝑿¯​𝚼~(1))a​b=∑c​dX¯a​b​c​d​Υ~c​d(1),\left(\bar{\bm{X}}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}\right)_{ab}=\sum_{cd}{\bar{X}}_{abcd}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{(1)}_{cd}, (242a)
also 3-rank tensors 𝒁¯\bar{\bm{Z}}, 𝒁′¯\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}} are contracted on the last two indices:
(𝒁¯​𝚼~(1))a=∑b​cZ¯a​b​c​Υ~b​c(1).\left(\bar{\bm{Z}}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}\right)_{a}=\sum_{bc}\bar{Z}_{abc}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{(1)}_{bc}. (242b)
The 3-rank tensor 𝑿′′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}} is contracted only on the last index:
(𝑿′′¯​𝓡~(1))a​b=∑b​cX¯a​b​c′′​ℛ~c(1).\left(\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}}{\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}\right)_{ab}=\sum_{bc}\bar{X}^{\prime\prime}_{abc}{\tilde{\mathcal{R}}}^{(1)}_{c}. (242c)

The 2-rank tensor 𝒁′′¯\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime\prime}} is contracted on the last index, as the standard matrix rows-by-columns product.

The explicit expression of the coefficients in 𝑿¯\bar{\bm{X}}, 𝒀¯\bar{\bm{Y}}, 𝒁¯\bar{\bm{Z}}… is reported in Appendix H.

The tensors introduced in Eq. (241c) account for the free time-evolution of the system with the full anharmonic interaction: they are defined by the static unperturbed Hamiltonian ℋ^​[ρ]{\hat{\mathcal{H}}}[\rho]. In particular, they depend on phonon scattering vertexes: the 4-phonon scattering tensor 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}} and 3-phonon scattering tensor 𝑫(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}, and the free evolution 𝑫(2)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(2)}}}{\bm{D}}. Due to the Gaussian constrain on the density matrix, the TD-SCHA does not account directly for higher-order phonon scattering processes. However, 𝑫(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}, 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}, and 𝑫(2)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(2)}}}{\bm{D}} depend “self-consistently” on higher-order anharmonicities, as they are averaged on the equilibrium distribution. In fact, they are temperature dependent.

In particular, 𝑿¯\bar{\bm{X}} and 𝑿′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}} depend on 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}, while 𝒁¯\bar{\bm{Z}}, 𝒁′¯\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}} and 𝑿′′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}} depend on 𝑫(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}. The 𝑿¯\bar{\bm{X}}, 𝑿′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}, 𝒀¯\bar{\bm{Y}}, 𝒀′¯\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}} and 𝒁′′¯\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime\prime}} contain terms of the free evolution, that are non zero even if the system is a perfect harmonic crystal. Table 1 summarizes these dependencies.

The 𝑫(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} and 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}} terms are obtained from the 𝚽(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{\Phi}} and 𝚽(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{\Phi}} when transforming in the mass-rescaled variables.

D(3)a​b​c=Φ(3)a​b​cma​mb​mc\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}_{abc}=\frac{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\Phi}_{abc}}{\sqrt{m_{a}m_{b}m_{c}}} (243)
D(4)a​b​c​d=Φ(4)a​b​c​dma​mb​mc​md\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}_{abcd}=\frac{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\Phi}_{abcd}}{\sqrt{m_{a}m_{b}m_{c}m_{d}}} (244)

Appendix I Proof of the dynamical ansatz

Here we compute the TD-SCHA self energy:

𝓖−1​(ω)=(𝒁′′+ω2)−𝚷⁡(ω)\bm{{\mathcal{G}}}^{-1}(\omega)=({\bm{Z}}^{\prime\prime}+\omega^{2})-\bm{\Pi}(\omega)

By looking at Eq. (253), 𝚷⁡(ω)\bm{\Pi}(\omega) is obtained by how the last row interact with the rest of the big 𝑮⁡(ω)\bm{G}(\omega) matrix through 𝑿′′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}}.

The complete one-phonon green function is given by Eq. (89).

𝒢μ​ν​(ω)=(00𝜹𝝁)​(𝑿¯+ω2𝒀¯𝒁¯𝑿′¯𝒀′¯+ω2𝒁′¯𝑿′′¯0𝒁′′¯+ω2)−1​(00𝜹𝝂).{\mathcal{G}}_{\mu\nu}(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\bm{\delta_{\mu}}\end{pmatrix}{\begin{pmatrix}\bar{\bm{X}}+\omega^{2}&\bar{\bm{Y}}&\bar{\bm{Z}}\\ \bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}&\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2}&\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}}\\ \bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}}&0&\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime\prime}}+\omega^{2}\end{pmatrix}^{-1}}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\\ \bm{\delta_{\nu}}\end{pmatrix}. (253)

Thus, the self-energy is

𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑿¯′′​∂𝚼~(1)∂𝓡~(1)​(ω)\bm{\Pi}(\omega)={\bar{\bm{X}}}^{\prime\prime}\frac{\partial{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}}{\partial{\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}}(\omega) (254)

Here, products between tensors follows the same convention as Eq. (242c), where the number of indices to be contracted is determined by the tensor on the left. The inversion of a 4-rank tensor is equivalent of inverting a matrix where we group the first two and last two indices:

X¯a​b​c​d=X¯(a​b)​(c​d).\bar{X}_{abcd}=\bar{X}_{(ab)(cd)}. (255)

and 𝑿′′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}} is contracted with the indices of 𝚼~(1){\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}. In particular, this term indicates how a perturbation in the quantum fluctuations 𝚼~(1){\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)} affects the average positions 𝓡~(1){\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}. If 𝑫(3)≠0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}\neq 0, the dynamics in 𝓡~(1){\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)} affects 𝚼~(1){\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)} and Re​𝑨~(1)\mathrm{Re}{\tilde{\bm{A}}}^{(1)} through 𝒁¯\bar{\bm{Z}} and 𝒁′¯\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}} (Eq. 241a and 241b). They evolve freely (harmonic propagation) and interacting anharmonically through 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}. Finally, 𝚼~(1){\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)} affects back 𝓡~(1)\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}^{(1)} through 𝑿′′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}} (Eq. (241c)).

To calculate 𝚷⁡(ω)\bm{\Pi}(\omega), we need to get an explicit expression from the dependency of 𝚼~(1){\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)} and 𝓡~(1){\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}. It is convenient to remove the Re​𝑨~(1)​(ω)\mathrm{Re}{\tilde{\bm{A}}}^{(1)}(\omega) firstly (Eq. 241b):

𝑿′¯​𝚼~(1)+(𝒀′¯+ω2)​Re​𝑨~(1)+𝒁′¯​𝓡~(1)=0\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}+(\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2})\mathrm{Re}{\tilde{\bm{A}}}^{(1)}+\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}}{\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}=0 (256)
Re​𝑨~(1)=−(𝒀′¯+ω2)−1​(𝑿′¯​𝚼~(1)+𝒁′¯​𝓡~(1)).\mathrm{Re}{\tilde{\bm{A}}}^{(1)}=-(\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\left(\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}+\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}}{\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}\right). (257)

We substitute it in the 𝚼~(1)​(ω){\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}(\omega) equation (Eq. 241a):

[(𝑿¯+ω2)−𝒀¯​(𝒀′¯+ω2)−1​𝑿′¯]​𝚼~(1)+\displaystyle\left[(\bar{\bm{X}}+\omega^{2})-\bar{\bm{Y}}(\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}\right]{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}+
+[𝒁¯−𝒀¯​(𝒀′¯+ω2)−1​𝒁′¯]​𝓡~(1)=0\displaystyle+\left[\bar{\bm{Z}}-\bar{\bm{Y}}(\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}}\right]{\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}=0 (258)

From which we get the relationship between 𝚼~(1)​(ω){\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}(\omega) and 𝓡~(1)​(ω){\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}(\omega).

The final result we get is:

𝚷⁡(ω)=−𝑿′′¯\displaystyle\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=-\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime\prime}} [(𝑿¯+ω2)−𝒀¯(𝒀′¯+ω2)−1𝑿′¯]−1⋅\displaystyle\left[(\bar{\bm{X}}+\omega^{2})-\bar{\bm{Y}}(\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}\right]^{-1}\cdot
⋅[𝒁¯−𝒀¯​(𝒀′¯+ω2)−1​𝒁′¯]\displaystyle\cdot\left[\bar{\bm{Z}}-\bar{\bm{Y}}(\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\bar{\bm{Z}^{\prime}}\right] (259)

Now, we prove that the previous equation correspond to the dynamical ansatz proposed by Bianco et al.[47], reported in Eq. (92).

To simplify the expression, we define the tensor 𝑼\bm{U}, 𝑷\bm{P} and 𝑻\bm{T}, that in the polarization basis are:

X′′¯α​β​γ=Uα​β​D(3)α​β​γ\bar{X^{\prime\prime}}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}=U_{\alpha\beta}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma} (260)
𝑷=(𝑿¯+ω2)−𝒀¯​(𝒀′¯+ω2)−1​𝑿′¯\bm{P}=(\bar{\bm{X}}+\omega^{2})-\bar{\bm{Y}}(\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}+\omega^{2})^{-1}\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}} (261)
Tα​β=Z¯α​β​γD(3)α​β​γ−Y¯α​β​(Y′¯α​β+ω2)−1​Zα​β​γ′D(3)α​β​γT_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\bar{Z}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}}{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}}-{\bar{Y}}_{\alpha\beta}\left(\bar{Y^{\prime}}_{\alpha\beta}+\omega^{2}\right)^{-1}\frac{Z^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}}{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}} (262)

Both 𝑼\bm{U} and 𝑻\bm{T} are 2-rank tensors, while 𝑷\bm{P} is in general a 4-rank tensor. However, if 𝑫(4)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}=0 also 𝑷\bm{P} becomes a 2-rank tensor. For this reason it is easier to split 𝑷\bm{P} in two contribution:

𝑷=𝑷(0)+𝑷(1)\bm{P}={\bm{P}^{(0)}}+{\bm{P}^{(1)}} (263)

where 𝑷(0)=𝑷{\bm{P}^{(0)}}=\bm{P} if 𝑫(4)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}=0.

With this expression, the self-energy becomes:

𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑫(3)​𝑼​𝑷−1​𝑻​𝑫(3)\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}{\bm{P}}^{-1}\bm{T}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} (264)

Here, the inversion of the 4-rank 𝑷\bm{P} tensor is equal to the inversion of a big rank 2 tensor in which the first two and last two indices are grouped together. Moreover, 𝑻\bm{T} has only two indices even if in the right-hand expression of Eq. (262) three indices appears, as both Z¯α​β​γ\bar{Z}_{\alpha\beta\gamma} and Z′¯α​β​γ\bar{Z^{\prime}}_{\alpha\beta\gamma} loose the dependence on the γ\gamma index if divided by D(3)α​β​γ\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}.

First of all, lets consider the simple case for which 𝑫(4)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}=0 but 𝑫(3)≠0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}\neq 0. In this case the Bianco self-energy reduces to the bubble diagram:

𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑫(3)​𝚲​(ω)​𝑫(3)\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}\bm{\Lambda}(\omega)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} (265)

If we set 𝑫(4)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}=0 in our Eq. (264) we get:

𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑫(3)​𝑼​𝑷(0)−1​𝑻​𝑫(3)\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} (266)

The two equations are equal if:

𝚲⁡(ω)=𝑼​𝑷(0)−1​𝑻\bm{\Lambda}(\omega)={\bm{U}}{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}} (267)

This equality can be proved by a simple algebric calculations. In fact, 𝑷(0)\bm{P}^{(0)} is a diagonal 4-rank tensor in the polarization basis, and can be inverted by inverting its elements.

The explicit expression in the polarization basis of the 𝑻\bm{T}, 𝑷(0)\bm{P}^{(0)} and 𝑼\bm{U} are:

Uα​β=−ℏ2​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)8​ωα​ωβU_{\alpha\beta}=-\hbar^{2}\frac{(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)}{8\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}} (268)
Tγ​δ\displaystyle T_{\gamma\delta} =[(4​nγ+2)​ωδ+(4​nδ+2)​ωγℏ​(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)+8​ωγ​ωδ(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)(ω2−ωγ2−ωδ2)​(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)+2​ωγ​ωδ⋅\displaystyle=\bigg[\frac{(4n_{\gamma}+2)\omega_{\delta}+(4n_{\delta}+2)\omega_{\gamma}}{\hbar(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)}+\frac{8\omega_{\gamma}\omega_{\delta}}{(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)}\frac{(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\gamma}^{2}-\omega_{\delta}^{2})(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)+2\omega_{\gamma}\omega_{\delta}}\cdot
⋅(2​ωγ​nγ​(nγ+1)ℏ​(2​nγ+1)+2​ωδ​nδ​(nδ+1)ℏ​(2​nδ+1))]\displaystyle\cdot\left(\frac{2\omega_{\gamma}n_{\gamma}(n_{\gamma}+1)}{\hbar(2n_{\gamma}+1)}+\frac{2\omega_{\delta}n_{\delta}(n_{\delta}+1)}{\hbar(2n_{\delta}+1)}\right)\bigg] (269)
Tγ​δ\displaystyle T_{\gamma\delta} =[(4​nγ+2)​ωδ+(4​nδ+2)​ωγℏ​(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)+8​ωγ​ωδ(ω2−ωγ2−ωδ2)​(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)+2​ωγ​ωδ​(2​ωγ​nγ​(nγ+1)ℏ​(2​nγ+1)+2​ωδ​nδ​(nδ+1)ℏ​(2​nδ+1))]\displaystyle=\bigg[\frac{(4n_{\gamma}+2)\omega_{\delta}+(4n_{\delta}+2)\omega_{\gamma}}{\hbar(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)}+\frac{8\omega_{\gamma}\omega_{\delta}}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\gamma}^{2}-\omega_{\delta}^{2})(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)+2\omega_{\gamma}\omega_{\delta}}\left(\frac{2\omega_{\gamma}n_{\gamma}(n_{\gamma}+1)}{\hbar(2n_{\gamma}+1)}+\frac{2\omega_{\delta}n_{\delta}(n_{\delta}+1)}{\hbar(2n_{\delta}+1)}\right)\bigg] (270)
Pα​β(0)\displaystyle P_{\alpha\beta}^{(0)} =ω2−ωα2−ωβ2−2​ωα​ωβ(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)−8​ωα​ωβ(ω2−ωα2−ωβ2)​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)+2​ωα​ωβ⋅\displaystyle=\omega^{2}-\omega_{\alpha}^{2}-\omega_{\beta}^{2}-\frac{2\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}{(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)}-\frac{8\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\alpha}^{2}-\omega_{\beta}^{2})(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)+2\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}\cdot
⋅2​ωα​ωβ​(2​nα​nβ+nα+nβ)​(2​nα​nβ+nα+nβ+1)(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)\displaystyle\cdot\frac{2\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}(2n_{\alpha}n_{\beta}+n_{\alpha}+n_{\beta})(2n_{\alpha}n_{\beta}+n_{\alpha}+n_{\beta}+1)}{(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)} (271)
Pα​β(0)\displaystyle P_{\alpha\beta}^{(0)} =ω2−ωα2−ωβ2−2​ωα​ωβ(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)​[1+8​ωα​ωβ​(2​nα​nβ+nα+nβ)​(2​nα​nβ+nα+nβ+1)(ω2−ωα2−ωβ2)​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)+2​ωα​ωβ]\displaystyle=\omega^{2}-\omega_{\alpha}^{2}-\omega_{\beta}^{2}-\frac{2\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}{(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)}\left[1+\frac{8\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}(2n_{\alpha}n_{\beta}+n_{\alpha}+n_{\beta})(2n_{\alpha}n_{\beta}+n_{\alpha}+n_{\beta}+1)}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\alpha}^{2}-\omega_{\beta}^{2})(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)+2\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}\right] (272)

With some algebric manipulation, it is straightfoward to show that

Uα​β​Tα​βPα​β(0)=−ℏ24​ωα​ωβ[\displaystyle\frac{U_{\alpha\beta}T_{\alpha\beta}}{P^{(0)}_{\alpha\beta}}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{4\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}\bigg[ (ωα+ωβ)​(nα+nβ+1)(ωα+ωβ)2−ω2+\displaystyle\frac{(\omega_{\alpha}+\omega_{\beta})(n_{\alpha}+n_{\beta}+1)}{(\omega_{\alpha}+\omega_{\beta})^{2}-\omega^{2}}+
−(ωα−ωβ)​(nα−nβ)(ωα−ωβ)2−ω2]\displaystyle-\frac{(\omega_{\alpha}-\omega_{\beta})(n_{\alpha}-n_{\beta})}{(\omega_{\alpha}-\omega_{\beta})^{2}-\omega^{2}}\bigg] (273)

That is exactly the expression in the polarization basis of the 𝚲⁡(ω)\bm{\Lambda}(\omega) tensor. Therefore we proved Eq. (267), and the dynamical ansatz of Bianco in the case 𝑫(4)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}=0. To proceed with the case 𝑫(4)≠0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}\neq 0 we must add the 𝑷(1)\bm{P}^{(1)}.

𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑫(3)​𝑼​[𝑷(0)+𝑷(1)¯]−1​𝑻​𝑫(3)\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}\left[{\bm{P}^{(0)}}+\bar{\bm{P}^{(1)}}\right]^{-1}{\bm{T}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} (274)
𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑫(3)​𝑼​[𝟙+𝑷(0)−1​𝑷(1)¯]−1​𝑷(0)−1​𝑻​𝑫(3)\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}\left[\mathbbm{1}+{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}\bar{\bm{P}^{(1)}}\right]^{-1}{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} (275)

We already proved that

𝚲⁡(ω)=𝑼​𝑷(0)−1​𝑻\bm{\Lambda}(\omega)={\bm{U}}{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}} (276)

Therefore, it is trivial to show that Eq. (275) is the Bianco self-energy (Eq. 92) if we prove that:

𝑷(0)−1​𝑷(1)¯=𝑷(0)−1​𝑻​𝑫(4)​𝑼.{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}\bar{\bm{P}^{(1)}}={\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}. (277)

In fact, if we substitute Eq. (277) into Eq. (275), and we perform the Taylor expansion for small 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}, we get:

𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑫(3)​𝑼​𝑷(0)−1​𝑻​𝑫(3)+𝑫(3)​𝑼​𝑷(0)−1​𝑻​𝑫(4)​𝑼​𝑷(0)−1​𝑻​𝑫(3)+⋯\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}+\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}{\bm{U}}{\bm{P}^{(0)}}^{-1}{\bm{T}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}+\cdots
𝚷⁡(ω)=𝑫(3)​𝚲​(ω)​𝑫(3)+𝑫(3)​𝚲​(ω)​𝑫(4)​𝚲​(ω)​𝑫(3)+⋯\bm{\Pi}(\omega)=\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}\bm{\Lambda}(\omega)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}+\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}\bm{\Lambda}(\omega)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}\bm{\Lambda}(\omega)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}+\cdots (278)

That is the correct diagrammatic expansion of the self-energy, as defined in ref.[47].

We give here the explicit expression of the 𝑷(1)\bm{P}^{(1)} 4-rank tensor.

Pα​β​γ​δ(1)\displaystyle P^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} =−ℏ​(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)​(2​ωα​nβ+2​ωβ​nα+ωα+ωβ)4​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)​ωγ​ωδD(4)α​β​γ​δ−8​ωα​ωβ(ω2−ωα2−ωβ2)​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)+2​ωα​ωβ⋅\displaystyle=-\frac{\hbar(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)(2\omega_{\alpha}n_{\beta}+2\omega_{\beta}n_{\alpha}+\omega_{\alpha}+\omega_{\beta})}{4(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)\omega_{\gamma}\omega_{\delta}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}-\frac{8\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\alpha}^{2}-\omega_{\beta}^{2})(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)+2\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}\cdot
⋅ℏ​[ωα​nα​(nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)+ωβ​nβ​(nβ+1)​(2​nα+1)]​(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)4​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)​ωγ​ωδ​D(4)α​β​γ​δ\displaystyle\cdot\frac{\hbar\left[\omega_{\alpha}n_{\alpha}(n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)+\omega_{\beta}n_{\beta}(n_{\beta}+1)(2n_{\alpha}+1)\right](2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)}{4(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)\omega_{\gamma}\omega_{\delta}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} (279)
Pα​β​γ​δ(1)=−ℏ​(2​nγ+1)​(2​nδ+1)​D(4)α​β​γ​δ4​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)​ωγ​ωδ​[2​ωα​nβ+2​ωβ​nα+ωα+ωβ+8​ωα​ωβ​[ωα​nα​(nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)+ωβ​nβ​(nβ+1)​(2​nα+1)](ω2−ωα2−ωβ2)​(2​nα+1)​(2​nβ+1)+2​ωα​ωβ]P^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}=-\frac{\hbar(2n_{\gamma}+1)(2n_{\delta}+1)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}}{4(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)\omega_{\gamma}\omega_{\delta}}\left[2\omega_{\alpha}n_{\beta}+2\omega_{\beta}n_{\alpha}+\omega_{\alpha}+\omega_{\beta}+\frac{8\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}[\omega_{\alpha}n_{\alpha}(n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)+\omega_{\beta}n_{\beta}(n_{\beta}+1)(2n_{\alpha}+1)]}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\alpha}^{2}-\omega_{\beta}^{2})(2n_{\alpha}+1)(2n_{\beta}+1)+2\omega_{\alpha}\omega_{\beta}}\right] (280)

Again, with straightfoward algebra we can prove that:

Pα​β​γ​δ(1)Pα​β(0)=Tα​β​D(4)α​β​γ​δ​Uγ​δPα​β(0)\frac{P^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}}{P^{(0)}_{\alpha\beta}}=\frac{T_{\alpha\beta}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}U_{\gamma\delta}}{P^{(0)}_{\alpha\beta}} (281)

This concludes the proof that the one-phonon self-energy proposed as ansatz by Bianco et al.[47] can be formally derived in a full dynamical contex within the TD-SCHA.

Appendix J Harmonic two-phonon propagator

In this section we derive the Harmonic two-phonon propagator from the response system of Eq. (68).

The harmonic limit is obtained as 𝑫(3)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}}=0 and 𝑫(4)=0\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}}=0. In this limit, the one-phonon and two-phonon Green functions are decoupled. The two-phonon propagation is described by the variables Re​𝑨\mathrm{Re}\bm{A} and 𝚼\bm{\Upsilon}, so we isolate these contributions in the green function (Eq. (70)).

The two phonon green function is obtained inverting the matrix:

G(2​p​h)​(ω)=(−𝑿¯−ω2−𝒀¯−𝑿′¯−𝒀′¯−ω2)−1G^{(2ph)}(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}-\bar{\bm{X}}-\omega^{2}&-\bar{\bm{Y}}\\ -{\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}}}&-\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}}-\omega^{2}\end{pmatrix}^{-1} (282)

In the polarization basis, the tensor 𝑿¯\bar{\bm{X}}, 𝒀¯\bar{\bm{Y}}, 𝑿′¯\bar{\bm{X}^{\prime}} and 𝒀′¯\bar{\bm{Y}^{\prime}} are diagonal. Therefore, once we identify a couple of modes μ​ν\mu\nu, we only need to invert a 2x2 matrix in Eq. (282).

Since we are interested in the fluctuations-fluctuations correlation function, we only need the response in the 𝚼\bm{\Upsilon} block (the fluctuations are the convariance matrix 𝚼−1\bm{\Upsilon}^{-1}). This term is:

Gμ​ν(Υ)​(ω)=−Y′¯μ​ν​μ​ν−ω2X′¯μ​ν​μ​ν​Y¯μ​ν​μ​ν+(X¯μ​ν​μ​ν+ω2)​(Y′¯μ​ν​μ​ν+ω2)G^{(\Upsilon)}_{\mu\nu}(\omega)=\frac{-\bar{Y^{\prime}}_{\mu\nu\mu\nu}-\omega^{2}}{\bar{X^{\prime}}_{\mu\nu\mu\nu}\bar{Y}_{\mu\nu\mu\nu}+(\bar{X}_{\mu\nu\mu\nu}+\omega^{2})(\bar{Y^{\prime}}_{\mu\nu\mu\nu}+\omega^{2})} (283)

Subsittuting the expression defined in H (taking care of the symmetry exchanging μ↔ν\mu\leftrightarrow\nu) we get:

Ga​b(Υ)​(ω)\displaystyle G^{(\Upsilon)}_{ab}(\omega) =2ℏ​(4​na​nb+2​na+2​nb+1)⋅\displaystyle=\frac{2}{\hbar\left(4{n}_{a}{n}_{b}+2{n}_{a}+2{n}_{b}+1\right)}\cdot
⋅[−2​ω2​ωa​nb−ω2​ωa−2​ω2​ωb​na−ω2​ωb[(ωa−ωb)2−ω2]​[(ωa+ωb)2−ω2]+\displaystyle\cdot\bigg[\frac{-2\omega^{2}{\omega}_{a}{n}_{b}-\omega^{2}{\omega}_{a}-2\omega^{2}{\omega}_{b}{n}_{a}-\omega^{2}{\omega}_{b}}{[(\omega_{a}-\omega_{b})^{2}-\omega^{2}][(\omega_{a}+\omega_{b})^{2}-\omega^{2}]}+
+2​ωa3​nb+ωa3−2​ωa2​ωb​na−ωa2​ωb[(ωa−ωb)2−ω2]​[(ωa+ωb)2−ω2]+\displaystyle+\frac{2{\omega}_{a}^{3}{n}_{b}+{\omega}_{a}^{3}-2{\omega}_{a}^{2}{\omega}_{b}{n}_{a}-{\omega}_{a}^{2}{\omega}_{b}}{[(\omega_{a}-\omega_{b})^{2}-\omega^{2}][(\omega_{a}+\omega_{b})^{2}-\omega^{2}]}+
+−2​ωa​ωb2​nb−ωa​ωb2+2​ωb3​na+ωb3[(ωa−ωb)2−ω2]​[(ωa+ωb)2−ω2]]\displaystyle+\frac{-2{\omega}_{a}{\omega}_{b}^{2}{n}_{b}-{\omega}_{a}{\omega}_{b}^{2}+2{\omega}_{b}^{3}{n}_{a}+{\omega}_{b}^{3}}{[(\omega_{a}-\omega_{b})^{2}-\omega^{2}][(\omega_{a}+\omega_{b})^{2}-\omega^{2}]}\bigg] (284)

This green function has the poles in the correct position, when:

ω2=(ωa±ωb)2\omega^{2}=(\omega_{a}\pm\omega_{b})^{2}

Since we want the fluctuation-fluctuation correlation function, we need to change variable for the Green function from 𝚼\bm{\Upsilon} to 𝚼−1\bm{\Upsilon}^{-1}. This is achieved knowing how the perturbation in (𝚼−1)(1)(\bm{\Upsilon}^{-1})^{(1)} depend on those on 𝚼(1)\bm{\Upsilon}^{(1)}:

(𝚼−1)a​b(1)=−∑c​dΥa​c−1Υb​d−1Υc​d(1)(\bm{\Upsilon}^{-1})^{(1)}_{ab}=-\sum_{cd}\Upsilon^{-1}_{ac}\Upsilon^{-1}_{bd}\Upsilon^{(1)}_{cd} (285)

From this expression we can compute the fluctuation-fluctuation response function:

χa​b​c​d(ω)=Ga​b​c​d(Υ−1)(ω)=−∑e​fΥa​e−1Υb​f−1Ge​f​c​d(Υ)(ω)\chi_{abcd}(\omega)=G^{(\Upsilon^{-1})}_{abcd}(\omega)=-\sum_{ef}\Upsilon^{-1}_{ae}\Upsilon^{-1}_{bf}G^{(\Upsilon)}_{efcd}(\omega) (286)

If we substitute the expressions in the polarization basis, we obtain:

χμ​ν​(ω)\displaystyle\chi_{\mu\nu}(\omega) =−ℏ​(ωμ−ων)​(nμ−nν)2​(ω−ωμ+ων)​(ω+ωμ−ων)​ωμ​ων+\displaystyle=-\frac{\hbar\left({\omega}_{\mu}-{\omega}_{\nu}\right)\left({n}_{\mu}-{n}_{\nu}\right)}{2\left(\omega-{\omega}_{\mu}+{\omega}_{\nu}\right)\left(\omega+{\omega}_{\mu}-{\omega}_{\nu}\right){\omega}_{\mu}{\omega}_{\nu}}+
+ℏ​(ωμ+ων)​(nμ+nν+1)2​(ω2−(ωμ+ων)2)​ωμ​ων\displaystyle+\frac{\hbar\left({\omega}_{\mu}+{\omega}_{\nu}\right)\left({n}_{\mu}+{n}_{\nu}+1\right)}{2\left(\omega^{2}-\left({\omega}_{\mu}+{\omega}_{\nu}\right)^{2}\right){\omega}_{\mu}{\omega}_{\nu}} (287)

That is the standard two-phonon propagator.

Appendix K Additional details on the Lanczos algorithm

Here, we prove Eq. (130), and discuss the stochastic calculation of Eq. (132) as well as how we implemented symmetries in the Lanczos algorithm. If we have a perturbation vector

ρ(1)→(𝚼~(1)Re​𝑨~(1)𝓡~(1)),\rho^{(1)}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}\\ \ \mathrm{Re}{\tilde{\bm{A}}}^{(1)}\\ {\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}, (288)

the averages on the perturbed ensemble have been computed in Appendix G:

⟨d​𝕍d​Ra⟩ρ(1)=−12∑h​k​q​pΥ~h​k(1)Υ~k​p−1Υ~h​q−1D(3)q​p​a\left\langle\frac{d\mathbb{V}}{dR_{a}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{hkqp}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{(1)}_{hk}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{-1}_{kp}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{-1}_{hq}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}_{qpa} (289)
⟨d2​𝕍d​R~a​d​R~b⟩ρ(1)=∑cD(3)a​b​c​ℛ~c(1)−12​∑h​k​p​qΥ~h​k(1)​Υ~k​p−1​Υ~h​q−1​D(4)q​p​a​b\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{R}_{a}d\tilde{R}_{b}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}=\sum_{c}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{D}_{abc}{\tilde{\mathcal{R}}}^{(1)}_{c}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{hkpq}\tilde{\Upsilon}^{(1)}_{hk}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{-1}_{kp}{\tilde{\Upsilon}}^{-1}_{hq}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{D}_{qpab} (290)

Thus, substituting this expression inside the equation of the motion, it is straightforward to show that:

ℒanh​(𝚼~(1)Re~​𝑨(1)𝓡~(1))=(𝚼~​⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)+⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)​𝚼~Re​𝑨~​⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)+⟨d2​𝕍d​𝑹~​d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)​Re​𝑨~−⟨d​𝕍d​𝑹~⟩ρ(1)),{\mathcal{L}}^{\text{anh}}\begin{pmatrix}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}\\ {\tilde{\mathrm{Re}}\bm{A}}^{(1)}\\ {\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}+\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}\\ \mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}+\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}\mathrm{Re}\tilde{\bm{A}}\\ -\left\langle\frac{d{\mathbb{V}}}{d\tilde{\bm{R}}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}\end{pmatrix}, (291)

However, computing Eq. (290) by explicitly calculating both 𝑫(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} and 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}} is a terrible choice. The calculation of 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}} itself is challenging, as it must be computed with a stochastic average for each of the N4N^{4} elements, with a computational cost scaling as Nconf​N4N_{\text{conf}}N^{4}, prohibitive for systems with hundreds of atoms in the simulation cell.

Instead, we use the importance sampling to calculate these averages:

⟨d​𝕍d​R~a⟩ρ(1)=−⟨𝕗a​ρ(1)​(𝑹)ρ⁡(𝑹)⟩ρ\left\langle\frac{d\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{R}_{a}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}=-\left\langle\mathbbm{f}_{a}\frac{\rho^{(1)}(\bm{R})}{\rho(\bm{R})}\right\rangle_{{\rho}} (292)
⟨d2​𝕍d​R~a​d​R~b⟩ρ(1)\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{R}_{a}d\tilde{R}_{b}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}} =−∑cΥ~a​c⟨u~c𝕗~bρ(1)​(𝑹)ρ⁡(𝑹)⟩ρ\displaystyle=-\sum_{c}\tilde{\Upsilon}_{ac}\left\langle\tilde{u}_{c}\tilde{\mathbbm{f}}_{b}\frac{\rho^{(1)}(\bm{R})}{\rho(\bm{R})}\right\rangle_{{\rho}} (293)

where 𝕗\mathbbm{f} is the difference between the BO force 𝒇\bm{f} and the force of the equilibrium SCHA auxiliary Hamltonian

𝕗a​(𝑹)=fa​(𝑹)+∑b⟨d2​Vd​Ra​d​Rb⟩ρ​Rb,\mathbbm{f}_{a}(\bm{R})=f_{a}(\bm{R})+\sum_{b}\left\langle\frac{d^{2}V}{dR_{a}dR_{b}}\right\rangle_{{\rho}}R_{b}, (294)

and 𝒖=𝑹−𝓡\bm{u}=\bm{R}-\bm{\mathcal{R}} is the displacement from the average centroid position. We got Eq. (293) by integrating by parts, as done in ref.[47]. Thus, the averages are computed with new weights wi(1)w_{i}^{(1)} on each ionic configuration 𝑹{i}\bm{R}_{\{i\}}:

wi(1)=ρ(1)​(𝑹{i})ρ⁡(𝑹{i})w_{i}^{(1)}=\frac{\rho^{(1)}(\bm{R}_{\{i\}})}{\rho(\bm{R}_{\{i\}})} (295)

By Taylor expanding the density matrx, we get:

wi(1)=−12​𝒖~{i}​𝚼~(1)​𝒖~{i}+𝒖~{i}​𝚼~​𝓡~(1)+12​Tr​[𝚼~−1​𝚼~(1)].w_{i}^{(1)}=-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\bm{u}}_{\{i\}}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}\tilde{\bm{u}}_{\{i\}}+\tilde{\bm{u}}_{\{i\}}\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}{\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{R}}}}^{(1)}+\frac{1}{2}\textup{Tr}\left[{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{-1}{\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}}^{(1)}\right]. (296)

Since the last term is a constant factor that does not depend on the specific configuration, does not contribute to the averages; we remember that the averages of Eq. (292) and Eq. (293) are on the SCHA gradient for centroid positions and auxiliary force constants, thus any term of wi(1)w^{(1)}_{i} not depending on the configuration gives zero at equilibrium.

We compute Eq. (292) and Eq. (293) with a standard weighted average:

⟨d​𝕍d​R~a⟩ρ(1)=−1Nconf∑i=1Nconf𝕗a(𝑹{i})wi(1)\left\langle\frac{d\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{R}_{a}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}=-\frac{1}{N_{\text{conf}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{conf}}}\mathbbm{f}_{a}(\bm{R}_{\{i\}})w_{i}^{(1)} (297)
⟨d2​𝕍d​R~a​d​R~b⟩ρ(1)=−1Nconf∑i=1Nconf(∑cΥ~a​cu~c)𝕗b(𝑹{i})wi(1)\left\langle\frac{d^{2}\mathbb{V}}{d\tilde{R}_{a}d\tilde{R}_{b}}\right\rangle_{\rho^{(1)}}=-\frac{1}{N_{\text{conf}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{conf}}}\left(\sum_{c}\tilde{\Upsilon}_{ac}\tilde{u}_{c}\right)\mathbbm{f}_{b}(\bm{R}_{\{i\}})w_{i}^{(1)} (298)

Eq. (297) and (298), as well as the weights Eq. (296), require at most N2N^{2} operations for each configuration, granting an overall computational cost of Nconf​N2N_{\text{conf}}N^{2}.

The point group symmetries of a crystal are accounted for by unwrapping the stochastic ensemble. For each symmetry and configuration in the ensemble, we generate all the equivalent configurations according to the symmetry. The equivalent configuration is obtained by:

us⁡(a)α=∑β=13Sα​β​uaβu_{s(a)}^{\alpha}=\sum_{\beta=1}^{3}S^{\alpha\beta}u_{a}^{\beta} (299)

where s⁡(a)s(a) is where the atom equivalent to aa by the SS symmetry and Sα​βS_{\alpha\beta} is the symmetry matrix. In the same way, we obtain the BO force of the new configuration. Here, we make explicit the atomic lower index with Latin letters and Cartesian upper indices with the ancient Greek alphabet. In this way, the stochastic average is computed over a number of effective configurations equal to Nconf​Nsym​NTN_{\text{conf}}N_{\text{sym}}N_{T}, where NsymN_{\text{sym}} is the number of symmetries in the point-group and NTN_{T} is the number of translations inside the super-cell. Notably, symmetries cannot be applied on the final result itself of Eq. (297) and (298), as the perturbed vector ρ(1)​(𝑹)\rho^{(1)}(\bm{R}) violates point group symmetries.

The other symmetry not explicitly accounted for in Eq. (297) and (298) is that 𝑫(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\bm{D}} and 𝑫(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\bm{D}} are invariant under indices permutation. To enforce this symmetry we need to sum separately each part of the weights (Eq. 296) into the perturbed averages, and swapping the index of forces 𝕗\mathbbm{f} with the one of the displacements 𝚼~​𝒖~\tilde{\bm{\Upsilon}}\tilde{\bm{u}}.
